lesson.title: The TH → D Bridge
lesson.subtitle: brother → broeder, three → drie, think → denken

hook.title: English TH, Dutch D
hook.content: English kept the old th sound; Dutch hardened it to d. Brother is broeder, three is drie, think is denken, thank is danken. German did the same thing, but Dutch often kept a vowel closer to English.

pattern.title: The tongue stops hissing
pattern.content: Say brother and feel the tongue between the teeth. Now say broeder: the tongue has moved back and the sound has become a clean d. The same move turns three into drie and thing into ding.
pattern.linguist_note: The Germanic dental fricative /θ/ hardened to /d/ in Dutch and German but survived in English — one of the clearest family fingerprints.
pattern.trap_note: This is a recognition rule, not a conversion machine. Many Dutch d words have no English th twin at all; use the rule to spot twins, not to invent words.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (The TH → D Bridge):
exercises.target_answer: de broer, drie, denken, dank, het ding, ander
exercises.meaning: brother, three, to think, thanks, thing, other
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "The TH → D Bridge": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “My brother is here.”?
exercises.explanation: “Mijn broer is hier.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “The TH → D Bridge”.

cues: The pattern: The tongue stops hissing
It means: We think of the house.
exercises.explanation: “Wij denken aan het huis.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — The tongue stops hissing.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Ik dank je.” is word-for-word “I thank you.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: The tongue stops hissing.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: The thing is big.
exercises.explanation: “Het ding is groot.” reuses only material taught in “The TH → D Bridge” — The tongue stops hissing.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Het ding is groot.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising The tongue stops hissing.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “The other man is here.”
twist.explanation: Ander is the th→d twin of other; the adjective takes -e before a de-word.

summary.outcome: Recognise th↔d twins and use broer, denken, dank and ding in simple sentences.
summary.takeaway: The rule is a hint for recognition, not a licence to predict every d word.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: TH → D Discrimination.

broer.etymology_derivation: English brother and Dutch broer are cognate; Dutch shortened the word.

drie.etymology_derivation: English three and Dutch drie are the same word.

denken.etymology_derivation: English think and Dutch denken are the same verb; th hardened to d.

dank.etymology_derivation: English thank is the same root; Dutch d is the hardened th.

ding.etymology_derivation: English thing and Dutch ding are the same word.

ander.etymology_derivation: English other and Dutch ander are the same word; th hardened to d.

th_d.name: The TH → D Bridge
th_d.phonetic_rule: English th corresponds to Dutch d: brother → broeder, three → drie, think → denken, thank → danken.
th_d.historical_linguistics: The Germanic dental fricative hardened to a stop in Dutch and German; English kept the fricative.
th_d.philological_note: Weather/weer is cognate but Dutch lost the d, so it is not a th↔d example. Loans such as theater keep t.
